steps.say: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is the first choice operation for large kidney stones. Any renal stone bigger than 20 millimeters, any staghorn stone filling the branches of the kidney, and any lower pole stone bigger than 15 millimeters should go for PCNL. Smaller stones can pass or be treated with shock waves or a flexible scope, but bulky stone load needs a direct track through the back into the kidney.
steps.tx: **Percutaneous nephrolithotomy** (keyhole stone removal through a track in the back, abbreviated PCNL) is the gold standard first line treatment for **renal calculi larger than 20 mm** (two centimetres), **staghorn calculi** (large branched stones filling the renal pelvis and calyces), and **lower pole stones over 15 mm** (one and a half centimetres). Smaller stones suit shock wave lithotripsy or flexible ureteroscopy, while bulky stone load needs direct percutaneous clearance.

vis.alt: Plain KUB radiograph showing a dense radio opaque renal calculus in the kidney area.
vis.caption: Renal calculus on plain KUB: stones above 20 mm need PCNL rather than shock waves. Credit: University of Washington Virtual Patient.

steps.say: The surgeon reaches the stone through the posterior calyx, which is the cup of the kidney pointing backwards. The puncture follows the line of Brodel, a relatively bloodless plane where the front two thirds of the kidney meet the back one third. Staying on this line keeps the needle away from the large segmental arteries, so bleeding stays low and the track lands straight into the collecting system.
steps.tx: Obtain **renal access** (needle puncture track into the kidney) through the **posterior calyx** (back facing collecting cup) along the **avascular line of Brodel** (relatively bloodless plane at the junction of the anterior two thirds and posterior third of the kidney). This line avoids the major **segmental arteries** (large branch vessels of the renal artery), so puncture here keeps bleeding low and lands the sheath squarely inside the collecting system.

rows: Line of Brodel, anterior two thirds meets posterior third

steps.say: Upper pole stones are hard to reach from below, so the surgeon sometimes punctures above the twelfth or eleventh rib. This supracostal path gives a straight downhill run at the upper calyx and clears stones faster. The price is the chest: the needle can nick the pleura or lung, causing fluid or air around the lung in 5 to 15 percent of cases, so a chest film after surgery is routine.
steps.tx: **Supracostal access** (puncture above the 12th or 11th rib) gives a straight downhill run into **upper pole calculi** (stones in the top cup of the kidney) and clears them faster than a lower puncture. The trade off is chest injury, because the needle can nick the **pleura** (lung lining) or lung and cause **hydrothorax or pneumothorax** (fluid or air around the lung) in **5% to 15%** (five to fifteen in a hundred) of cases, so a postoperative chest film is routine.

steps.say: A standard PCNL track is wide, 24 to 30 French, which clears fragments fast but sacrifices more kidney tissue and blood. A mini PCNL uses a slim 14 to 20 French sheath, so blood loss and parenchymal trauma fall sharply while modern lasers still dust the stone effectively. Choose standard tracks for huge stone volumes and mini tracks for moderate stones or anaemic patients where every millilitre of blood counts.
steps.tx: **Mini-PCNL** (slim track stone surgery) uses a **14F to 20F sheath** (fourteen to twenty French calibre) and cuts **blood loss and parenchymal trauma** (kidney tissue injury) compared with standard **24F to 30F tracts** (twenty four to thirty French calibre), while laser **dusting** (breaking stone to fine powder) keeps clearance effective. Reserve wide standard tracts for huge stone volumes, and pick mini tracks for moderate stones or anaemic patients where blood conservation decides the plan.

points: Less blood loss and tissue trauma
Best for moderate stones, anaemic patients

steps.say: Not all stones are equal, so two scoring systems grade complexity before surgery. The Guy stone score runs from Grade I, a single simple stone, to Grade IV, a staghorn or complex branched stone, and higher grades predict lower stone free rates. The CROES nephrolithometric nomogram is calculated from stone burden, location, and patient factors, giving one objective number that forecasts clearance and supports honest counselling.
steps.tx: Stratify complexity with the **Guy stone score** (four grade complexity scale, Grades I to IV) and the **CROES nephrolithometric nomogram** (objective scoring tool predicting stone free rates). Grade I means a single simple stone and Grade IV means a **staghorn or complex branched stone** (stone filling pelvis plus multiple calyces), while higher grades predict lower clearance. The CROES tool folds **stone burden** (total stone volume), location, and patient factors into one number that forecasts outcome and guides consent.

rows: Grades I to IV, simple to staghorn
Predicts stone free rate, guides consent

steps.say: Bleeding is the commonest serious complication of PCNL because every track crosses kidney tissue. Most venous oozing stops with balloon tamponade, which means inflating a balloon inside the track to press on the bleeding wall. Severe arterial bleeding that keeps flowing despite tamponade is an emergency for selective transcatheter renal artery angioembolization, where an interventional radiologist threads a catheter to the bleeding branch and blocks it with coils.
steps.tx: Control track bleeding first with **conservative balloon tamponade** (balloon inflated inside the tract pressing on the bleeding wall), because most venous oozing settles with pressure. **Severe arterial bleeding** (brisk pulsatile blood loss) that fails tamponade needs prompt **selective transcatheter renal artery angioembolization** (catheter blockade of the bleeding branch with coils, done by an interventional radiologist). Never watch brisk arterial bleeding conservatively, because delayed blockade risks kidney loss and transfusion.

steps.say: Complex branched stones defeat a single approach, so endoscopic combined intrarenal surgery uses two surgeons at once. One surgeon passes a flexible ureteroscope upwards through the bladder while the other works downwards through the PCNL track, and the two meet inside the kidney. This dual attack reaches stones hiding in parallel calyces and pushes clearance of staghorn stones far above either route alone.
steps.tx: **Endoscopic combined intrarenal surgery** (simultaneous two route stone surgery, abbreviated ECIRS) pairs **retrograde flexible ureterorenoscopy** (scope passed upwards through the bladder and ureter) with **antegrade PCNL** (scope passed downwards through the back track) to maximise clearance of **complex branched calculi** (stones spread across parallel calyces). The two surgeons meet inside the kidney, so stones hiding from one route fall to the other, and staghorn clearance rises above either route alone.

vis.alt: Plain KUB radiograph showing a massive branched staghorn calculus filling the renal pelvis and calyces.
vis.caption: Staghorn calculus on KUB: branched stones filling pelvis and calyces need ECIRS dual route clearance. Credit: Craterib.

steps.say: Traditionally every PCNL ended with a thick nephrostomy tube draining the kidney through the back, which hurt and kept patients in hospital. In an uncomplicated case with complete stone clearance and minimal bleeding, tubeless PCNL skips the tube and leaves only a thin ureteral stent or catheter. Patients feel less pain, leave hospital sooner, and heal just as safely, so tubeless exit is now the default for clean straightforward cases.
steps.tx: **Tubeless PCNL** (finishing without a nephrostomy tube, leaving only a ureteral stent or catheter) is safe in **uncomplicated procedures** (complete stone clearance with minimal bleeding) and cuts pain and hospital stay. The traditional **nephrostomy tube** (thick back drain through the track) stays reserved for complicated cases with residual fragments, heavy bleeding, or collecting system injury. Choose tubeless exit as the default for clean straightforward cases, because healing matches tubed cases with far less discomfort.

rows: No nephrostomy tube, stent or catheter only
Residual fragments, heavy bleeding, system injury
